objects: Consider two disjoint circles x and y in a plane. They will serve as our witness since they do not satisfy C(x,y), O(x,y), P(x,y), PP(x,y), EQ(x,y), PO(x,y), TPP(x,y), EC(x,y), NTPP(x,y), Pi(x,y), PPi(x,y), NTPPi(x,y), or TPPi(x,y).

Consider two overlapping regions x and y. Since O(x,y), it follows that C(x,y) (Rule 2). Therefore, DC(x,y) is false and DR(x,y) is also false because they are not discrete from each other due to being connected.

Consider two regions x and y such that they touch only at their boundaries (EC relation). In this case, C(x,y) holds because they share a point. However, O(x,y) does not hold since they do not share any interior points. Also, PO(x,y) does not hold as there is no partial overlap.

Consider two regions x and y where they overlap (O(x,y)), but do not partially overlap (¬PO(x,y)). This satisfies the condition since O(x,y) is true, and PO(x,y) is false. C(x,y) must be true due to rule 2.

Consider two regions where x is part of y (P(x,y)), but they are not connected (\lnot C(x,y)). This satisfies the condition as it provides a witness for P(x,y) while negating at least one other predicate, in this case \lnot C(x,y).

Consider two overlapping regions where x is a part of y. This satisfies P(x,y). Since they overlap, they are connected (C(x,y)) and thus cannot be disconnected (DC(x,y)). Therefore, the condition \lnot DC(x,y) holds.

Consider two regions x and y such that x is a proper part of y (PP(x,y)). This means C(x,y), O(x,y), P(x,y) are true. However, we can choose x and y so that they do not satisfy EC(x,y). For example, if x is fully contained within y but does not touch the boundary of y, then NTPP(x,y) holds instead of EC(x,y).

Consider two regions x and y such that x is a proper part of y (PP(x,y)), but they are not discrete from each other, not non-tangential proper parts, nor non-tangential proper part inverses. This satisfies PP(x,y) and at least one negated condition.

Consider two regions x and y where x is a non-tangential proper part of y (NTPP(x,y)). Since NTPP(x,y), we know C(x,y), O(x,y), P(x,y), PP(x,y) are true. However, DR(x,y) can be false because they share interior points. Also, NTPPi(x,y) is the inverse relation and would not hold if x is a non-tangential proper part of y.

Consider two regions x and y where Pi(x,y) holds but none of the other predicates do. For example, if region y is a part of region x (y ⊂ x), then Pi(x,y) is true, but C(x,y), DC(x,y), O(x,y), P(x,y), PP(x,y), EQ(x,y), DR(x,y), PO(x,y), TPP(x,y), EC(x,y), NTPP(x,y), PPi(x,y), NTPPi(x,y), and TPPi(x,y) are all false.
x is a proper part of y (PPi(x,y)), x touches the boundary of y but does not overlap with its interior, and no other relations hold between them.

Consider regions x and y such that NTPPi(x,y) is true. This means C(x,y), O(x,y), Pi(x,y), and PPi(x,y) must be true, but P(x,y) and PP(x,y) are false since they are not required by the definition of NTPPi(x,y). Additionally, DR(x,y) and NTPP(x,y) can also be false. This satisfies the condition.

Consider two regions x and y where P(x,y) is true (x is part of y), but Pi(x,y) is also true (y is part of x). This implies that EQ(x,y) should hold. However, we need to find a case where at least one of the other predicates is false.

Consider two regions x and y that are connected (C) but do not overlap in their interiors (DR), yet share some interior points (O). This setup does not allow for P(x,y), PP(x,y), NTPP(x,y), or NTPPi(x,y) to be true, as they would imply a stronger relationship between x and y that contradicts the given conditions.

x and y are regions such that x partially overlaps with y (PO), x is part of y (P), they share interior points (O), and they are connected (C). This satisfies the conditions without violating any rules, as DC(x,y) is false.
Consider regions x and y where x is a non-tangential proper part inverse (NTPPi) of y. This means that C(x,y), O(x,y), P(x,y), and NTPPi(x,y) are true, but PP(x,y) and NTPP(x,y) are false.
x and y are regions that touch at their boundaries but do not share any interior points, they partially overlap, and x is not a part of y nor vice versa.

Consider two regions x and y where x is a larger region that contains y as its non-tangential proper part (NTPPi). They overlap but do not share any interior points, making them discrete from each other. Since NTPP(x,y) must be false for the statement to hold true, we have found our witness.

Consider regions x and y where x is a larger region containing y, but their boundaries do not touch (NTPPi(x,y)). They share some interior points but neither is fully part of the other (PO(x,y)), and they are connected (C(x,y)) and overlap (O(x,y)). This satisfies all positive conditions. Since NTPPi(x,y) holds true, at least one negated condition must be false, satisfying the overall statement.

Consider regions x and y where x is a non-tangential proper part inverse of y (NTPPi(x,y)), they are connected (C(x,y)), overlapped (O(x,y)), and x is a part of y (P(x,y)). Since PO(x,y) holds, it means that x and y share some interior points but neither is fully a subset of the other. Given these conditions, we can satisfy at least one negated predicate such as \lnot DC(x,y).

Consider two regions x and y where they are connected (C) but do not share all interior points (O), they are discrete from each other (DR), partially overlapped (PO), and NTPPi(x,y). Since DR is satisfied, DC cannot be true. The negated predicates ensure that at least one of them will hold.
